title: Exercise 7A · Q7
summary: Two right angles share the side QS: find QS in ΔPQS, then SR in ΔQSR.
alt: Exercise 7A · Q7: In the figure, ∠PQS = ∠QSR = 90°. Given that PQ = 45 cm, QR = 30 cm and PS = 53 cm, find the length of (i) QS, (ii) SR.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In the figure, **∠PQS = ∠QSR = 90°**. **PQ = 45 cm**, **QR = 30 cm** and **PS = 53 cm**. We have to find (i) **QS** and (ii) **SR**.

steps.title: Spot the right angle
steps.narration: In ΔPQS, **∠Q = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **PS**. The other two sides meet at the right angle.

steps.title: Pythagoras' theorem
steps.narration: **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PS^2} &= \role{legA}{PQ^2} + \role{legB}{QS^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Make the unknown the subject
steps.narration: We want a **shorter side**, so subtract the known square from the hypotenuse square.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PS^2} &= \role{legA}{PQ^2} + \role{legB}{QS^2} \\ \role{legB}{QS^2} &= \role{hyp}{PS^2} - \role{legA}{PQ^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute the lengths
steps.narration: Replace each side by its length.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PS^2} &= \role{legA}{PQ^2} + \role{legB}{QS^2} \\ \role{legB}{QS^2} &= \role{hyp}{PS^2} - \role{legA}{PQ^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{53^2} - \role{legA}{45^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: Take the square root of both sides (a length is positive).\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PS^2} &= \role{legA}{PQ^2} + \role{legB}{QS^2} \\ \role{legB}{QS^2} &= \role{hyp}{PS^2} - \role{legA}{PQ^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{53^2} - \role{legA}{45^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{2809} - \role{legA}{2025} \\ &= \role{legB}{784} \\ \role{legB}{QS} &= \sqrt{784} = \role{ans}{28\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔQSR, **∠S = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **QR**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. (QR is the hypotenuse of this second triangle.) **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QR^2} &= \role{legA}{QS^2} + \role{legB}{SR^2} \\ \role{legB}{SR^2} &= \role{hyp}{QR^2} - \role{legA}{QS^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QR^2} &= \role{legA}{QS^2} + \role{legB}{SR^2} \\ \role{legB}{SR^2} &= \role{hyp}{QR^2} - \role{legA}{QS^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{30^2} - \role{legA}{28^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{900} - \role{legA}{784} \\ &= \role{legB}{116}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 116 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QR^2} &= \role{legA}{QS^2} + \role{legB}{SR^2} \\ \role{legB}{SR^2} &= \role{hyp}{QR^2} - \role{legA}{QS^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{30^2} - \role{legA}{28^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{900} - \role{legA}{784} \\ &= \role{legB}{116} \\ \role{legB}{SR} &= \sqrt{116} = \role{ans}{10.8\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Hypotenuse?
challenges.prompt: In **ΔQSR** (right angle at S), which side is the **hypotenuse**?
challenges.hint: It is opposite the right angle.
challenges.explain: The right angle is at S, so the hypotenuse is the opposite side QR.

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
